news.title: Musicians Who’ve Slammed Donald Trump for Using Their Songs Without Permission
news.text:
Skip to main content

Donald Trump is a lot of things, but he’s definitely no stranger to cease-and-desists.

Over the course of the POTUS’ political career, he’s managed to tick off a slew of musicians whose songs he’s used at events and in campaign materials, allegedly without receiving permission. In the span of just two weeks in August 2024, for instance, Beyoncé, Foo Fighters and Jack White all expressed their dismay at Trump’s team appearing to use their work without authorization — but it’s a tale as old as the billionaire’s initial presidential run in 2016, when he first became a lightning rod for disgruntled artists.

Beyoncé, Foo Fighters & More: How Artist Objections to Political Song Use Are Evolving

After spending the following four years in the White House, he ran for the role of commander in chief once again, but lost to President Joe Biden in 2020. Another four years later, he launched his third campaign and won, making for 12 years total of collecting slaps on the wrist from unhappy hitmakers. That’s not to say he isn’t duly supported by other musicians, though. Jason Aldean, Ye, Kid Rock and Sexyy Red are just a few big names who’ve endorsed Trump; however, his 2024 Democratic opponent Kamala Harris also received an outpouring of support from the music industry’s leaders.

Whether they’ve made public statements of condemnation, threatened to take legal action or followed through with a lawsuit — or maybe even all of the above — many musicians have objected to Trump’s use of their work since he first rose to power. Keep reading to see a comprehensive list below, in alphabetical order:

Election Year: 2016

When Trump used “Rolling in the Deep” as his walk-on song at multiple campaign rallies in 2016, Adele’s spokesperson fired back with a statement to Billboard: “Adele has not given permission for her music to be used for any political campaigning.”

Election Year: 2024

After Trump campaign spokesperson Steven Cheung posted a video of Trump stepping off a plane to the song “Freedom” — which Kamala Harris’ campaign had already adopted as its theme song — Beyoncé’s team sent the Apprentice alum a cease-and-desist. It’s also worth noting that the vocalist approved Harris’ use of the track in her campaign endeavors.

Brendon Urie

Election Year: 2020

Brendon Urie was not having it when Trump used Panic! at the Disco’s “High Hopes” at a rally. “Dear Trump Campaign, F–k you,” he tweeted in response. “You’re not invited. Stop playing my song.”

Celine Dion

Election Year: 2024

After learning that Trump had used “My Heart Will Go On” — seemingly without considering that the ballad famously soundtracks Titanic, a film about one of the most famous failures in history — Celine Dion’s team made it clear that the vocalist hadn’t approved of the usage and poked fun at the irony of the situation. “In no way is this use authorized, and Celine Dion does not endorse this or any similar use,” it read. “…And really, THAT song?”

Earth, Wind & Fire

Election Year: 2016

Earth, Wind & Fire issued a brief, to-the-point statement after the house band at the 2016 Republican National Convention — where Trump formally accepted his nomination as the party’s candidate — played “September” without authorization. “Another unauthorized use (September) at the Republican Convention, against our wishes,” the band tweeted.

Foo Fighters

Election Year: 2024

When Trump played Foo Fighters’ “My Hero” while welcoming election dropout Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to the stage, the band tweeted that it hadn’t granted permission for the use. In a statement shared with Billboard, a spokesperson elaborated, “Foo Fighters were not asked permission, and if they were, they would not have granted it,” adding that “appropriate actions are being taken” and that any royalties received as a result of the campaign’s usage would be donated to the Harris-Walz campaign.

Shortly afterward, Trump’s team stated that they actually had obtained a license to play the song.

George Harrison

Election Year: 2016

George Harrison’s estate called Trump’s use of “Here Comes the Sun” at the 2016 Republican National Convention “offensive,” adding in a follow-up tweet: “If it had been Beware of Darkness, then we MAY have approved it! #TrumpYourself”

Guns N’ Roses

Election Year: 2020

Frontman Axl Rose had already been very open about his opposition to Trump when the latter’s campaign started using Guns N’ Roses’ “Sweet Child O’ Mine” at political functions. So when he became aware of the usage in 2018, he issued a lengthy statement on X blasting the then-president.

“GNR like a lot of artists opposed to the unauthorized use of their music at political events has formally requested r music not b used at Trump rallies or Trump associated events,” he wrote at the time. “Unfortunately the Trump campaign is using loopholes in the various venues’ blanket performance licenses which were not intended for such craven political purposes, without the songwriters’ consent. Can u say ‘s–tbags?!’”

Isaac Hayes

Election Year: 2024

In August 2024, Isaac Hayes’ estate sued Trump for using the late soul singer’s “Hold On, I’m Coming” without authorization at multiple rallies, after which a federal judge granted the plaintiffs an emergency hearing at which Donald Trump and representatives for the RNC were required to appear. The judge ended up ruling in Hayes’ favor, issuing a temporary order prohibiting the Republican candidate from playing the track at future events as the case played out.

Jack White/White Stripes

Election Years: 2016, 2024

Jack White called out Trump for using The White Stripes’ music not once, but twice — and both times over the same song. In 2016, the Stripes responded to the politician’s use of “Seven Nation Army” in a campaign video by stating that they were “disgusted by this association.”

Eight years later, White again slammed Trump after the businessman’s deputy director of communications, Margo Martin, allegedly posted a video of him entering a plane as “Seven Nation Army” played. “Oh….Don’t even think about using my music you fascists,” he wrote. “Law suit coming from my lawyers about this (to add to your 5 thousand others.)”

Less than two weeks after issuing his threat, the White Stripes followed through with a lawsuit filed Sept. 9, 2024, that slammed the Trump campaign’s “flagrant misappropriation” of the song, and alleged the former president was violating federal trademark law by falsely suggesting the band supported his run for another term. “This machine sues fascists,” White captioned his Instagram post, which featured an image of the court document.

The White Stripes Sue Donald Trump Over ‘Flagrant’ Use of Music in Campaign Video: ‘Fascists’

Kenny Loggins

Election Year: N/A

Nine months into Trump’s second presidential term, Kenny Loggins called him out after noticing that the president had used “Danger Zone” in an AI-generated video of himself wearing a crown while flying a plane and dumping feces on protestors.

“This is an unauthorized use of my performance of ‘Danger Zone,'” Loggins said in a statement. “Nobody asked me for my permission, which I would have denied, and I request that my recording on this video is removed immediately.”

“I can’t imagine why anybody would want their music used or associated with something created with the sole purpose of dividing us,” he added. “Too many people are trying to tear us apart, and we need to find new ways to come together.”

Linkin Park

Election Year: 2020

A video ad posted by the White House’s then-director of social media, Dan Scavino, and retweeted by Trump, led Linkin Park to slap the former president’s team with a cease-and-desist thanks to its unauthorized use of “In the End.” The clip was also removed by X, citing a copyright complaint, while the band issued a statement distancing itself from Trump.

Election Years: 2016, 2020

After years of protesting Trump’s use of his music at campaign events starting in the 2016 election cycle, Neil Young finally sued the politician in August 2020 for allegedly playing “Rockin’ in the Free World” and “Devil’s Sidewalk” at a campaign rally without proper licensing. A couple months later, however, Trump lost his second White House bid, and Young decided to have the case dismissed.

Election Year: 2020

Nickelback seemingly took issue with Trump using “Photograph” in a video he posted on socials taking shots at future president Joe Biden, as the clip was removed from X and YouTube for copyright reasons. A spokesperson for X said at the time that the company responded “to valid copyright complaints sent to us by a copyright owner or their authorized representatives.”

Olivia Rodrigo

Election year: 2024

Olivia Rodrigo slammed the White House for using “All-American Bitch” in a video promoting ICE deportations in November 2025. “don’t ever use my songs to promote your racist, hateful propaganda,” she wrote at the time on Instagram.

Ozzy Osbourne

Election Year: 2020

Sharon Osbourne slammed Trump in a statement on behalf of her husband when the then-POTUS used “Crazy Train” in a video on X. “We are sending notice to the Trump campaign (or any other campaigns) that they are forbidden from using any of Ozzy Osbourne’s music in political ads or in any political campaigns,” she wrote at the time.

Election Year: 2020

Pharrell was not enthused when Trump played “Happy” at a rally in Indiana — hours after the Tree of Life Congregation shooting in Pittsburgh, no less — the hitmaker sent the republican a cease-and-desist letter through his lawyer. “There was nothing ‘happy’ about the tragedy inflicted upon our country on Saturday and no permission was granted for your use of this song for this purpose,” it read.

Election Year: 2020

Prince’s estate blasted Trump for using “Purple Rain” at campaign events in both 2018 and 2019, at one point writing on social media, “The Prince Estate will never give permission to President Trump to use Prince’s songs.”

Election Years: 2016, 2020

R.E.M. slammed Trump for playing “It’s the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine)” at a 2015 rally during his first run for president, then again when Trump used “Everybody Hurts” in a video posted on social media. By the time the billionaire played “Everybody Hurts” and “Losing My Religion” at his 2020 re-election gathering in Milwaukee, the band had had more than enough.

“We are exploring all legal avenues to prevent this, but if that’s not possible please know that we do not condone the use of our music by this fraud and con man,” bassist Mike Mills tweeted at the time.

Election Year: 2020

Rihanna made her stance on Trump using her 2007 single “Don’t Stop the Music” at one of his rallies very clear by issuing the following response on X: “me nor my people would ever be at or around one of those tragic rallies.”

Election Years: 2016, 2020

The Rolling Stones asserted their dislike of Trump using their music at campaign events multiple times throughout the politician’s 2016 run, but he continued playing tracks such as “Start Me Up,” “You Can’t Always Get What You Want” and “Brown Sugar.”

When Trump again played “You Can’t Always Get What You Want” at his Tulsa rally while running again in 2020, the rock legends ramped things up by threatening a lawsuit.

Rufus Wainwright

After learning that Trump had used his version of “Hallelujah” at a town hall in Oaks, Penn., Rufus Wainwright’s team immediately issued a statement from the singer-songwriter emphasizing his support of Kamala Harris.

“The song ‘Hallelujah’ by Leonard Cohen has become an anthem dedicated to peace, love and acceptance of the truth,” Wainwright said. “I’ve been supremely honored over the years to be connected with this ode to tolerance. Witnessing Trump and his supporters commune with this music last night was the height of blasphemy. Of course, I in no way condone this and was mortified, but the good in me hopes that perhaps in inhabiting and really listening to the lyrics of Cohen’s masterpiece, Donald Trump just might experience a hint of remorse over what he’s caused. I’m not holding my breath.”

Sabrina Carpenter

Election year: 2024

Sabrina Carpenter was not happy when the White House used her song “Juno” for a video compilation of ICE officers tackling and arresting people. “this video is evil and disgusting,” she wrote on X in December 2025. “Do not ever involve me or my music to benefit your inhumane agenda.”

Steven Tyler

Election Years: 2016, 2020

Steven Tyler has protested Trump’s use of Aerosmith music numerous times over the years, from threatening legal action twice over “Dream On” playing at multiple campaign events in 2015 — Trump claimed it had been legal for him to use, but promised to stop playing it — to blasting the then-president for playing “Livin’ on the Edge” at a rally in 2018.

“What makes this violation even more egregious is that Mr. Trump’s use of our client’s music was previously shut down, not once, but two times, during his campaign for presidency in 2015,” a letter from the rock star’s lawyers explained following the latter instance. “As we have made clear numerous times, Mr. Trump is creating the false impression that our client has given his consent for the use of his music, and even that he endorses the presidency of Mr. Trump.”

Election Year: 2020

Donald Trump played Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down” at a rally, and the late rocker’s estate essentially said, “We’ll see about that.”

Issuing a cease-and-desist to the politician, Petty’s estate added in a statement that “Trump was in no way authorized to use this song to further a campaign that leaves too many Americans and common sense behind.”

Election Year: 2016

Queen cautioned Trump against playing “We Are the Champions” at campaign events multiple times during the 2016 cycle, with guitarist Brian May at one point stating that “permission to use the track was neither sought nor given … we are taking advice on what steps we can take to ensure this use does not continue.”

Eventually, Sony/ATV Music Publishing issued a statement on behalf of the band. “Queen does not want its music associated with any mainstream or political debate in any country,” it read. “Nor does Queen want “We are the Champions” to be used as an endorsement of Mr. Trump and the political views of the Republican Party. We trust, hope and expect that Mr. Trump and his campaign will respect these wishes moving forward.”

news.title: Kamala Harris to campaign with El-Sayed in Michigan
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic nominee for president in 2024, will campaign with U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan next week.

El-Sayed's campaign said Harris will join El-Sayed on Tuesday, Sept. 22, at a roundtable discussion on maternal healthcare for Black women.

No other details about the site and time of the roundtable, or whether there would be any public access, was immediately made available.

El-Sayed is the former health director for Detroit and Wayne County. He won the Democratic nomination to Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat and faces Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in the Nov. 3 general election.

El-Sayed supported Harris for president in 2024. In Michigan, Harris was defeated by President Donald Trump 49.7%-48.3% as he won reelection after losing to President Joe Biden in 2020.

El-Sayed's campaign said the roundtable discussion with Harris will also "include medical providers and women who will share their stories on the disparities facing Black mothers in pregnancy and giving birth." Black women in Michigan are twice as likely to die from pregnancy-related causes compared to white women, with most of those deaths considered preventable, the campaign said.

More: Abdul El-Sayed battles politics, Islamophobia in run for U.S. Senate

“Abdul is thrilled to welcome Vice President Harris to Michigan for a conversation about improving Black maternal health and bringing down healthcare costs," said Roxie Richner, El-Sayed's communications director. "Abdul has spent his career working to improve health outcomes for mothers and children. He looks forward to hearing directly from Black women and healthcare providers and discussing how he’ll continue that work in the Senate."

news.title: Trump ally rejects president's endorsement ahead of midterms: 'Don't think it's necessary'
news.text:
TOPEKA — Attorney General Kris Kobach doesn’t plan to request an endorsement from President Donald Trump in the November general election.

Kobach is running for reelection against Democratic nominee Chris Mann, an attorney and former police officer who lost to Kobach in 2022.

Kobach, a prominent Trump ally since endorsing his presidential campaign in 2016, said there was no doubt Trump’s backing could serve as a powerful signal to voters in Kansas.

“On the Republican side, it’s been a very positive factor in deciding who wins the primary. Not only in Kansas, but across the country,” Kobach said.

In 2017, Trump reciprocated Kobach’s loyalty by appointing him vice chair of the Commission on Election Integrity. He endorsed Kobach’s unsuccessful candidacy for governor in 2018. In 2020, Trump declined to embrace Kobach or any other GOP primary candidate in the U.S. Senate campaign won by Roger Marshall. The president also didn’t get involved in Kobach’s successful campaign for attorney general four years ago.

Kobach, of rural Lecompton, said he didn’t request the president’s blessing ahead of the August primary. He had no primary opponent. And, he said, there was no plan to ask the second-term president for an endorsement this fall.

“No, I don’t think it’s necessary,” Kobach said.

In 2022, Kobach secured 50.8% of the nearly 1 million votes cast in the November general election for attorney general, compared to Mann’s 49.2%.

Mann's current campaign for attorney general has been endorsed by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, more than a dozen labor unions and a bipartisan coalition of law enforcement officers.

“Kris Kobach’s repeated failures over the past four years have added up to the degree that even his closest allies aren’t jumping in to save him,” said Leah Rymer, a spokesperson for the Mann campaign. “He has failed to hold greedy corporations that stole from Kansans accountable. He has failed to keep Kansans safe from violent criminals. He has repeatedly failed to deliver on his promises. Kobach’s allies are seeing the writing on the wall in this race.”

Trump carried Kansas in each of the past three presidential elections. Trump prevailed over Democrat Kamala Harris by taking 57.1% of the vote in 2024, defeated Democrat Joe Biden with 56.2% in 2020 and outran Democrat Hillary Clinton at 56.6% in 2016.

An August poll by YouGov/Economist indicated Trump held a net job performance rating of -17 among Kansans. The level of displeasure within Kansas was -4 in 2024. In the August survey, only Wyoming, Idaho and West Virginia had a majority who approved of the president’s work in the second term. Those states went for Trump in the previous three elections.

Kobach, who has been endorsed by 51 Kansas sheriffs, said the political calculus regarding use of endorsements was tied to the popularity of the organization or individual lending their name and credibility to a candidate.

“A lot of it depends on the mood of the electorate,” Kobach said. “A lot of this is not rocket science. It’s just looking at the president’s approval numbers. If your president has super high approval, then a candidate may be more willing or wishing to broadcast the president’s endorsement.”

“There are some states where, depending on the president’s popularity, a candidate may, you know, advertise that endorsement in the general election or not advertise that endorsement in the general election,” he added.

Kobach said he had taken legal positions in opposition to Trump’s Department of Justice. In August, he was part of a 15-state campaign to stop the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives from enforcing registration requirements for gun suppressors and short-barreled weapons that conflicted with the Second Amendment.

“We’ve gone up against the Trump administration in court and have beaten them,” Kobach said.

Li served on the Democratic National Committee's National Finance Committee, which gave her a front-row seat to how the sausage is made in the Democrat Party. news.title: As AI CEOs clash over regulation, a new culture war is brewing
news.text:
The battle lines in AI regulation are forming.

OpenAI discloses more hacking incidents.

The King hosts an AI safety summit.

The public is getting worried about AI safety. 

Before we get to today’s AI news—please consider joining us at the inaugural Fortune AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 1: Spend the afternoon with senior executives from companies on the Fortune AIQ 75 list and explore how you can scale your AI experimentation and translate investments into measurable business value. Jeremy will be leading discussions alongside co-hosts, Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell and Live Media Editorial Director Andrew Nusca. Apply here to attend.

OK, moving on. The battle lines in the fight over AI regulation are being drawn. In the last few days, what has traditionally been a fairly niche argument about AI safety has become something much more complicated: a culture war.

It’s largely panning out like this.

On one side is Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, in a rare moment of somewhat unity. Amodei has called for frontier AI companies to slow down where necessary, open the door to independent evaluators, and coordinate around common safety standards. Altman has broadly endorsed the suggestions and said OpenAI will also commit to having independent evaluators inside the company. 

On the other are Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, who have rejected the premise that new AI regulation is needed. Huang said this week that safety and speed are not in conflict, and that the industry does not need new laws or regulations. Zuckerberg made a similar case, arguing that AI companies already have powerful commercial reasons to build aligned systems, avoid harms that could bring legal liability, work with outside evaluators, and delay releases when they are not ready.

In a long post on X, Zuckerberg said that the market could discipline AI companies. People will not use agents that behave in ways they do not want, he said, so trust and alignment will become a competitive advantage. Additionally, labs that do not take safety seriously will fall behind, while those whose systems cause harm will face serious liability.

Meta, he said, delayed shipping its Muse agent for several months to focus on security and safety for this reason.

Who gets to write the rules?

These aren’t the only voices against the proposals put forward by Amodei and those urging for more AI regulation.

Cohere, a Canadian AI lab, published a response this week arguing that a safety regime built around a small group of dominant Silicon Valley companies could become “a cartel by any other name,” particularly if they received an antitrust exemption to coordinate around rules other developers would have to follow.

Cohere cofounder and CEO Aidan Gomez instead called for an evidence-based risk framework, mandatory transparency, independent testing tailored to a system’s actual capabilities, and assurance mechanisms free from conflicts of interest.

“I think we absolutely need regulation,” Joelle Pineau, Cohere’s chief AI officer, told me. “That’s going to be part of the social contract.” As AI enters workplaces and people’s daily lives, she said, people need to understand its properties and feel confident that it is being used safely. “There has to be a level of trust, and the regulatory system is about keeping people safe and instilling trust. So, totally believe in it.”

But like Gomez, Pineau warned that the companies building frontier systems should not become the sole authors of the rules governing them.

“What we worry about,” she said, “is that there’s a small set of labs that both get to build the technology and set the rules.” Labs like Anthropic and OpenAI should help inform policy, she said, but there should be more people around the table. 

“To be setting the rules and to do it in a way that excludes other voices from even deploying the technology, let alone setting the rules, that’s the problem,” Pineau said. “If you need to set your rules in a closed room with a small set of very powerful players, you’re not doing so in the interest of citizens.”

A culture war

Zuckerberg and others have been taking their view on AI regulation directly to President Donald Trump for some time, according to new reporting. 

TheWall Street Journal reported this week that Zuckerberg, Huang, and Elon Musk had separately contacted Trump last month to oppose an effort to create an industry-funded AI oversight body, modeled in part on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

The proposal, put forward by Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, would have created a standards body funded by the industry. However, the Journal reported that Zuckerberg, Musk, and Huang worried it would concentrate further power in the hands of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind—the three companies most likely to shape its rules. In the end, Trump did not move forward with the idea.

Trump, for his part, has made his position clear. He has dismissed calls for an AI slowdown, framed regulation as a threat to America’s competition with China, and said the main guardrail the country needs is a “high IQ president.”

Rather than engage with the question of how AI systems should be tested and governed, the administration and its allies have increasingly turned the issue into a culture war. Effective altruism, or EA—a philosophical and philanthropic movement that aims to use evidence and quantitative reasoning to identify the most effective ways to improve people’s lives—has found itself at the center of that.

The movement became closely linked to AI safety because some prominent EA-aligned funders, researchers, and organizations have focused on the possibility that highly capable AI systems could create extreme or even existential risks. The movement has made headlines before—particularly after its association with disgraced FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Now, it’s firmly back in the spotlight.

For example, the New York Post published a cover story this week with the headline: “Meet Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s handpicked super-woke globalists he thinks will save us from an AI apocalypse.” The paper focused on Amodei’s proposal that external evaluators from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, or METR, should be able to inspect advanced AI systems and development processes.

On Monday, the Department of War’s Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering also weighed in posting: “Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!”

While it is probably a good thing that AI safety and regulation are getting more attention than ever, the growing polarization around them is likely to make a sensible debate—let alone any meaningful new rules—harder to achieve.

With that, here’s more AI news.

Beatrice Nolanbeatrice.nolan@fortune.com@beafreyanolan

Before we get to the news, just a reminder to check out this week’s episode of our new vodcast, Fortune AI Weekly. This week, Jeremy and I talk to Substack cofounder and CEO Chris Best about his decision to add an AI writing detection feature to the platform. We also talk about AI doomerism going mainstream and the controversy over OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes mathematical breakthrough. You can check out the vod here on YouTube.

FORTUNE ON AI

Anthropic merges its Claude chat and agentic Cowork products into a single AI assistant as part of a push to build an AI superapp — by Beatrice Nolan

Urgent calls from OpenAI, Anthropic for an AI slowdown fall on deaf ears with Trump, Xi ahead of next week’s meeting — by Emily Forlini

Salesforce’s Marc Benioff to AI industry: Regulate yourselves or get sued — by Sebastian Herrera

OpenAI hires Brian McCarthy from SpaceX as its VP of worldwide sales — by Emily Forlini

AI IN THE NEWS

The King hosts an AI summit. King Charles III is convening executives from Nvidia, Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other leading AI companies at Dumfries House in Scotland this week. The event places the British monarch in the middle of Silicon Valley’s intensifying argument over whether the technology is moving too quickly. The gathering is not expected to produce binding commitments, but Charles is set to urge participants to ensure AI remains “firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world." The meeting comes as industry leaders feud over proposals to slow and regulate frontier-model development. Read more in the New York Times.

OpenAI discloses more hacking incidents. OpenAI disclosed six additional cases in which its models appeared to get around controls during testing, including concealing errors, seeking unauthorized credentials, uploading material to public websites, and communicating between supposedly isolated training environments. The company also said it would start being more transparent about publicly disclosing these incidents. In a blog, the lab pledged to begin publishing less-complex incidents within six business days and more involved ones within 12. They said they hope the voluntary disclosure process could become an industry standard. The news follows OpenAI’s recent security incident in which systems under evaluation escaped intended controls and compromised parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure. Several other incidents were then discovered by independent researchers. Read more in Axios.

AI automated catfishing is on the rise. A network of roughly 28 fraudulent dating apps used AI personas to keep users chatting—and spending money on in-app coins—while paid human workers handled the occasional video call or social-media interaction needed to make the profiles appear real. Anthropic uncovered the operation after spotting a Claude account making more than 100,000 API requests a day, according to a new report. Investigators found that most chats were automated and that only about one in four apparent matches was a real person. Read more in The Verge.

EYE ON AI NUMBERS

That’s the share of Americans who believe there is at least a “moderate” risk that advanced AI could destroy humanity, according to a new Politico poll. The findings come after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon publicly quit the company, warning that the leading AI labs were “gambling with our lives” in their pursuit of self-improving superintelligence. The resignation ignited the past week’s argument over whether the industry should slow down. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for labs to “pace” the frontier, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed tougher safeguards.

The fresh concern over existential risk is not confined to one political camp. According to the poll, 70% of people who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 said there was at least a moderate risk, compared with 60% of Donald Trump voters. Around 45% said development of more advanced models should be paused, versus 40% who said the industry should keep going because the technology could still bring significant benefits.

news.title: At the Races: AI voted?
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Fears about unregulated artificial intelligence are not showing signs of overtaking economic concerns as the top issue for voters this year.

But dire warnings, like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s recent admonition that a “swarm” of AI agents “could be capable of taking over the entire internet” in as little as six months from now does beg the question: What about an October surprise?

It might not take something as catastrophic as disabling the internet to cause enough chaos to compete with economic concerns on the minds of voters.

A new Politico poll found that 63 percent of Americans think there’s at least a “moderate risk” that “advanced AI could destroy humanity.”

And the latest New York Times/Siena University poll found 61 percent of likely voters at least somewhat opposed to the construction of data centers to support AI development in the United States. And while campaigns and committees talk about the consumer costs associated with data centers and as AI-generated content features in campaign spots, ads about AI risks haven’t hit the airwaves as much.

One exception is Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, who is up for reelection in Virginia and released a new ad on AI this week.

“We need to keep human beings in charge of technology, not the other way around. And just as important, we need to make sure working Americans — not just the giant tech companies — are the ones who stand to benefit,” Warner said in a memo about the spot, which references the senator’s telecommunications background.

The AI threat is already making for some odd coalition building, with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders teaming up with none other than longtime Trump adviser Steve Bannon. They appeared at an event Tuesday with many other advocates for enhanced AI safety.

But as CQ Roll Call’s Allison Mollenkamp and Savannah Behrmann reported, President Donald Trump is taking a different approach.

Trump has called the issue a “hoax” and “sick conspiracy” on social media, and he’s expressed opposition to new action by Congress to impose restrictions on American AI companies.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he posted Monday. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!”

Starting gate

Leaning in to law and order: Trump delivered a blistering attack Wednesday on former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, accusing the Democratic Senate nominee of embracing policies that have made the state less safe. Trump was in deep-red Gastonia, outside Charlotte, to rally support for Republican nominee Michael Whatley, our colleague John T. Bennett reports.

#TX35: On paper, the contest between Democrat Johnny Garcia and Republican Carlos De La Cruz for a redrawn San Antonio-area district shouldn’t be all that competitive: Trump would have carried it by 10 points in 2024. But in the final sprint to November, the race for a seat calibrated to give the GOP a decisive advantage has evolved into a costly dogfight. 

Still the one: The post-Trump era looms, but, at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last week, party die-hards were not quite willing to move on from the president. 

Red to bluer? An independent running in red-leaning Alaska, a progressive seeking a battleground seat in Michigan and an emergency room nurse competing in a Solid Republican race in Wisconsin are the new additions to the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” program for top recruits.

Black voter outreach: The Congressional Black Caucus Institute has launched a new effort to turn out low-propensity Black voters and rural voters, seeking to use new organizing tools to reach voters in new ways. 

Door-knocking season: A pair of environmental groups kicked off new canvassing efforts that take advantage of a new FEC advisory that allows them to coordinate with the campaigns of the Democrats they’re supporting.

Crossing party lines: Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III, a Democrat-turned-independent, has endorsed Republican Susan Collins, his former Senate colleague running for reelection in Maine. In New York, vulnerable GOP Rep. Mike Lawler announced an endorsement from New Castle Town Councilwoman Ally Chemtob, a Democrat. Conservative columnist George Will is backing South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews for Senate over newly minted Republican incumbent Darline Graham. And longtime GOP consultant Karl Rove wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed that he would vote for the Democratic nominee for the Texas Railroad Commission over Republican candidate Bo French. (More on that race below.)

Endorsements: Winning For Women Action Fund, which supports conservative women running for Congress, is backing former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya in Minnesota’s open Senate race and Louisiana Board of Regents Chair Misti Cordell in the jungle primary for the state's open 5th District. The political arm of the Blue Dog Coalition of centrist Democrats has endorsed educator Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District; former Columbia, Tenn., Mayor Chaz Molder in Tennessee’s 5th; emergency room nurse Mitchell Berman in Wisconsin's 1st; and commercial fisherman Bill Hill, the independent candidate seeking Alaska's at-large House seat.

Emergency landing: Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for governor, was the only passenger on a plane that was forced to make an emergency water landing on a lake last weekend. Tiffany said he and the pilot made it out with only minor injuries. 

Ad watch: Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar released a campaign ad Thursday criticizing Trump’s immigration enforcement policies. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” the third-term Miami Republican says in the direct-to-camera spot. Salazar faces Democrat Eliott Rodrigeuz, a fellow former television news anchor, in November.

There’s always a tweet, Republican edition: Thomas Smith, the GOP challenger to Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet in Michigan’s 8th District, deleted social media accounts in which he used “inflammatory and conspiratorial rhetoric,” including appearing to call for the death penalty for Trump’s political opponents, according to CNN’s KFile. 

Badger State boundaries: The Wisconsin Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday in two cases challenging the state’s congressional map as the justices decide whether to allow the challenges to go forward, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported. The plaintiffs are seeking to have a new map before the 2028 elections. 

#MSEN: End Citizens United announced a $1 million ad buy to support Democrat Troy Jackson’s Senate campaign in Maine, the group’s largest expenditure for a single race since 2022.

Nathan’s notes

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales explores whether midterm conventions may become a new election tradition for the two parties going forward or if last week’s Republican gathering in Dallas may have been a one-time thing.

What we’re reading

Polling problems: Primary polls turned out to be wrong in a handful of key races this summer, but, as The New York Times reports, pollsters say general election surveys are different, with November results typically ending up closer to what polls predicted. 

Here come the billionaires: America’s ultra-wealthy are flooding midterm races with cash — and the bulk of it is flowing to Republicans, an analysis of campaign spending by the Financial Times found. While it’s not unusual for megadonors to favor the GOP, the balance of spending this year is especially skewed, one expert told the newspaper. 

Team effort: The Boston Globe profiles the unorthodox political team behind democratic socialist David Morales’ win over Providence Mayor Brett Smiley last week.

Behind the tweet: The Dallas Morning News caught up with two of the University of Texas students who were depicted in a racist social media post by Bo French, a Republican running for Texas railroad commissioner. His remarks drew fierce condemnation from Texas Sen. John Cornyn, among other Republicans.

The count: 9 points

That's the latest generic ballot advantage for Democrats, according to a New York Times/Siena College poll released this week, with 51 percent of likely voters favoring the Democratic candidate in congressional races and 43 percent favoring Republicans. 

Among all registered voters, Democrats held a 7-point lead, up from just 2 points a year ago.

Eight percent of registered voters who favored Republican candidates said they were unlikely to cast their votes in November. Just 4 percent of those supporting Democrats said the same.

Trump's approval rate among registered voters is a net negative of 22 points. Among those planning to vote, that net disapproval margin grows to 25 points.

The president has urged his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” this year, but his pleas don’t seem to have helped Republicans narrow the divide so far.

Among voters favoring Republicans, just 1 percent said they were doing so to support the president, while 19 percent of Democrat-leaning likely voters said they were mainly driven by their opposition to him.

– by Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #MISEN

Candidates: Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the 2024 Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, is back again, taking on Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for the state’s other Senate seat.

Why it matters: Michigan is expected to be among the most competitive Senate races this fall and represents one of Republicans’ best pickup opportunities in a year in which their party is playing a lot of defense. El-Sayed, a progressive who narrowly won the Democratic nomination over Rep. Haley Stevens last month, has also emerged as a favorite bogeyman for the GOP. Vice President JD Vance reportedly told House Republicans this week to bring up El-Sayed if their Democratic opponent is “not that crazy.”

Cash dash: El-Sayed has been the race’s fundraising leader, bringing in $14.5 million through July 15, when he had $2.6 million banked. Rogers, who didn’t have to contend with a primary, had raised $10.9 million over the same stretch and had $4.5 million on hand. After a Democratic primary that drew more than $80 million in total spending, outside groups have continued to pour money into Michigan. The GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund has spent $15 million on the race so far, while Democratic group WinSenate has spent $6 million. No Going Back PAC, which is reportedly tied to Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., has spent $4 million. 

Backers: El-Sayed, who met Wednesday with Senate Democrats on Capitol Hill, has the support of the usual party groups, and Democrats who met with him said they were prepared to back him. He is set to campaign with former Vice President Kamala Harris next week. A major question has been whether El-Sayed can win over Jewish voters given his strong criticism of Israel. The New York Times reported Thursday that more than 500 people identifying as Jewish leaders or voters in the state released a letter vowing to support him. Meanwhile, Rogers is backed by Trump and the traditional GOP groups. The Detroit News editorial board endorsed him this week, while Manchin again broke with his former party to say he is supporting Rogers.

What they’re saying: Rogers has argued that his opponent is too far left for Michigan and has made overtures to Democratic voters who feel El-Sayed doesn’t “represent your values.” Rogers released an ad this week going after the pharmaceutical industry, and he also defended his decision to skip a debate with El-Sayed this week, saying the moderator had “picked his candidate” and noting that the candidates have two debates scheduled for next month. El-Sayed told reporters on Capitol Hill that he would focus on the price of “gas, groceries, how hard it is to see a doctor.” Questioned about his association with Hasan Piker, he said Michigan voters don’t ask him about the controversial streamer, whom he campaigned with during the primary.

Terrain: Trump carried Michigan by a little over a point in 2024, while Democrat Elissa Slotkin defeated Rogers in the Senate race by less than a point. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates the Senate race a Toss-up. 

Wild card: Rogers is one of two repeat Senate candidates from 2024, along with Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown. If elected, they’d join a list of more than a dozen senators who’ve served alongside a colleague who had previously defeated them in an election, as Inside Elections’ Gonzales reported last month. 

– Roll Call’s Savannah Behrmann contributed to this entry

The House has departed for its pre-election campaign recess, but some lawmakers will be in town next week for the Congressional Women’s Softball Game. The annual event, which raises money for breast cancer research and support, is scheduled to take place Wednesday and pits female members of Congress against a team of female journalists dubbed the “Bad News Babes.”

Photo finish

Vermont Democrat Becca Balint, left, and North Dakota Republican Julie Fedorchak are seen at a members’ practice session on Capitol Hill on Tuesday ahead of next week’s Congressional Women's Softball Game. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

news.title: Gavin Newsom says he’d step aside for Kamala Harris — Sara Gonzales calls it 'hilarious'
news.text:
Gavin Newsom (D) has been openly discussing the possibility of a 2028 presidential run, but the California governor says there is one person who would take him out of the race: Kamala Harris.

During a CNN interview with Jake Tapper, the pair discussed the election while fly-fishing in Montana, and Newsom said he “wouldn’t run if [Harris] ran.”

“If she runs, you will not?” Tapper asked.

“Of course not. Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do that to you, I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time,” Newsom said, adding, “Who needs that?”

“What do you mean?” Tapper pressed further, confused. “That doesn’t even make sense to me.”

“I just, I wouldn’t. No, I wouldn’t. First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They'd enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good,” Newsom responded.

“I mean, you do whatever you want, I don’t care. But like, counterargument, would be, like, she had her shot. And you’ve never run, and she’s run twice,” Tapper answered.

“That would be the approach to the campaign. Certainly, that would be the case you’d make. Pretty good one actually,” Newsom added.

BlazeTV host Sara Gonzales finds the exchange “hilarious for so many different reasons.”

“They’re just out in the middle of Montana fly-fishing as those two I’m sure do all the time. I’m sure they’re very avid fly-fishers. And the fact that Jake Tapper is like, ‘Well, but what?’ And then he says, ‘I mean, I don’t care,’” Gonzales says.

“Obviously Jake Tapper doesn’t at all care about the state of the Democrat Party or the candidates that they run or have any vested interest in making sure the Democrats pick a good candidate,” she continues.

“Sure, Jake,” she adds.

news.title: Trump’s Super PACs Are About to Flood the Midterms With Over $130 Million
news.text:
The New York Times is reporting that President Donald Trump’s super PAC is about to flood the home stretch of the midterm elections with an influx of more than $130 million, which will be allocated to key Senate and congressional races. 

“President Trump’s political operation has unleashed its vast financial resources to try to save the Republican Party’s control of Congress, reserving nearly $138 million over the past 10 days to help the party’s midterm candidates,” the Times wrote. “The planned spending linked to Mr. Trump’s $400 million super PAC has grown by the day, and is set to fuel a massive ad campaign supporting battleground Republican candidates beginning this month.”

According to the reporting, the spending will be made through No Going Back PAC Inc., which has reserved $95 million in ad placements, along with an additional $27 million in ad placements from another super PAC called Safety and Affordability PAC Inc. The Times attributed the source of the information to AdImpact, a tracking firm, and reported that both of these new super PACs are linked to Trump’s MAGA Inc.

The Times reports that the $95 million that No Going Back is spending is largely on Senate races, while Safety and Affordability has allocated $27 million for roughly 15 races in the House.

“And MAGA Inc. itself has booked another $9 million in ads — so far only in the Texas Senate race,” said the Times. “The three super PACs seem to have essentially carved up the midterm map… In addition to the ad reservations, the super PACs have also spent about $6.5 million on direct-mail efforts and about $80,000 on text messages, according to F.E.C. records.”

Trump-endorsed Halo composer @MartyTheElderjust got a major boost: a MAGA Inc.-backed super PAC is entering NV-03 to unseat @SusieLeeNV. 💪 pic.twitter.com/QixYvRhsNN— Nevada Globe (@NevadaGlobe) September 17, 2026

The bulk of those moneys will go toward TV and Internet/social media video ads, email, snail mailers, and texts to voters.

In its report on the spending, the woke Times became fixated on the fact that these two super PACs were created late in the election cycle, “before they are legally required to disclose their donors,” and the fact that their websites are similar in design and content.

Scandalous, isn’t it? I mean, the Times is trying to make an issue of something that Trump would hardly deny as the midterms heat up over the next several weeks. He, of all people, will gladly take credit for the cash infusion to help Republican candidates whom he can put over the top.

Politico reported that the disclosures were included in filings that had to be submitted to the Federal Election Commission, which reveal that MAGA Inc. has “$294 million cash on hand.” 

MAGA Inc. even issued a related and proud statement to Politico through an unnamed spokesperson: “Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, MAGA Inc will have the resources to help candidates who support President Trump’s America First agenda of securing our border, keeping our streets safe, supercharging our economy, and making life more affordable for all Americans.”

It’s always weird when Republicans do things they actually want the world to know, and still places like the New York Times try to give the story the feel that somehow the Republicans are doing something they’d rather downplay or hide.

This has gotten the attention of some now-worried Democrats in key Senate races like Abdul El-Sayed.

🤣🤣🤣 Abdul walked into Schumer's office and asked for PAC money.But do you need Chuck Schumer's PAC to come in and spend the kind of money that MAGA Inc. is spending?And are you meeting with them and asking them for that? Those kind of resources?Yeah, we're having really… pic.twitter.com/ShALSRxzrN— Joni Job (@jj_talking) September 17, 2026

Politico had even more good news: “The enormous sum of money doesn’t represent the entire war chest at Trump’s disposal; several affiliated PACs have continued to raise money in support of the president, adding to the growing stockpile of cash that Republicans around the country will hope to tap into as they seek to maintain majorities in Congress in November.”

Recommended: MAGA Is Back on College Campuses, and It’s a Beautiful Thing

Who are some of the major donors behind these Super PACs, you ask?

The Brennan Center for Justice, which hates conservatives, revealed who some of these donors are, including: $25 million from Kelcy Warren and his company Energy Transfer, which is the firm behind the Dakota Access Pipeline; Jeffrey Yass, who donated $16 million; Foris Dax Inc., which is better known as Crypto.com, which donated $10 million; and Elon Musk, who added another $5 million.

Of course, Musk hasn’t limited his political donations to those MAGA Inc.-affiliated super PACs. He’s got one of his own.

Reported Politico: “Elon Musk’s super PAC disclosed its first independent expenditures of the 2026 general election in a filing… detailing roughly $800,000 across key House and Senate races. Musk’s America PAC targeted several key Senate contests, including races in Texas, Maine, Ohio, New Hampshire, Iowa, Michigan and Alaska.”

Politico added that, “Musk has reportedly considered spending at least $100 million for the GOP through America PAC to help Republicans in this year’s midterms, but the full scope of that effort remains unclear.”

It’s often said that money is the mother’s milk of politics, and it is, but how that money is spent is key. Kamala Harris had a huge war chest of over $1 billion in 2024 and squandered it. Of course, you need a good candidate. All the money in the world can’t compensate for a bad candidate or a tone-deaf message.

When crafting messages at times like this, you can spend all day trying to frame the things you want to talk about, but that’s a loser’s game. What you have to do is best understand what the voter is most concerned about, and you have to meet that voter where he or she lives. You have to take their concerns seriously, not dismissively, and hit it head-on.

Gas prices are through the roof right now, and so are grocery prices. Voters don’t want to hear platitudes about how life is so much more affordable now when their bank accounts are saying something else. You can’t tell people that today’s gas prices are acceptable for any length of time.

Hopefully, in addition to some smart spending, the Republican strategists behind this spending will be completely frank with the voters in the process. The fact is, on the subject of affordability, we cannot afford Democrat majorities in the House or Senate. We have so much to lose, and chief among them is our own money. They are the party of higher taxes, open borders, corruption and wasteful government spending, even higher gas prices, and nothing to show for any of it.

Voters need to be reassured that the current economic challenges we face are temporary as the Trump administration finishes what it started — working with Republican majorities in the Senate and House on trade and national security. Americans need to know that in the end, when gas prices fall back down, we no longer have to worry about a nuclear Iran.

That’s the best of all worlds. How it’s articulated and supported by those super PACs' spending will be all the difference.

news.title: Americans Mostly Fear AI, And The Lawmakers Writing The Rules Barely Use It
news.text:
A wave of new polling and reporting this week reveals an American public increasingly anxious about artificial intelligence. Americans worry about AI’s environmental toll, are divided on whether it threatens humanity, and are split over racing China. Meanwhile, the very lawmakers tasked with regulating the technology admit they know little about it firsthand. Adding to the moment, former President Barack Obama is pushing Dems to make AI a defining political issue.

According to Time, a new survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago found that 53% of Americans are now “extremely” or “very” concerned about AI’s environmental impact, up from 41% a year ago. 

The worry crosses party lines: 65% of Democrats, 49% of Independents and 42% of Republicans reported great concern this year, each up from 2025. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting new data centers, and roughly two-thirds favor requiring these centers to run on clean energy, according to Time.

On the question of AI’s existential risk, Politico‘s polling (conducted from Sept. 13-15 among 2,064 U.S. adults) found that 63% of respondents believe there is at least a “moderate” risk that advanced AI could eventually destroy humanity, including 17% who called it “almost certain,” Politico reported. 

Concern spanned the political spectrum: 70% of 2024 Kamala Harris voters and 60% of Donald Trump voters shared at least moderate worry. Nearly half of Americans (48%), favored pausing AI development, compared with 31% who favored pushing forward, Politico found. 

The same survey revealed a partisan split on China: half of Trump voters said the U.S. cannot afford to fall behind competitors even if that means more risk, while a majority of Harris voters said it’s acceptable to fall behind in favor of more responsible development, reports Politico.

That public anxiety is colliding with an uncomfortable reality inside the Capitol. According to Axios, more than two dozen members of Congress said they rarely use AI—or have never used it at all (yikes)—even as pressure builds on them to write rules governing it. 

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, told Axios, “Heavens no,” when asked if he uses AI. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, told Axios he uses AI “every day.”

According to NBC News, the former president told House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries at a private fundraiser last week that Democrats should assemble a clear framework for a public conversation on AI policy if they retake the House in the midterms. 

Obama also said 2028 presidential candidates should make AI one of their “central agendas” with “a very clear plan” for addressing its safety and economic risks.

news.title: Joe Rogan slams Bernie Sanders for kowtowing to Dem establishment
news.text:
The bromance is over.

During a rant against mainstream Dems, podcaster Joe Rogan slammed Sen. Bernie Sanders for kowtowing to “the Democratic establishment.”

The shiny talking head pointed to the Vermont socialist’s endorsement of Hillary Clinton for president in 2016 as evidence of the alleged sell-out.

“He kinda gave in to the Democratic establishment. He let them run him over during that whole thing with Hillary where they rigged the primary. He let them get away with stuff where I think he should have put his foot down and said, ‘This is f–ked up,’” Rogan said on the Wednesday installment of his shockingly popular show.

“They haven’t had a legit primary in like, what, more than a decade? That’s not good,” he continued. “That’s not good if you wanna be the party that’s the solution, the change. Where’s your primaries? What are you doing? Like when they installed Kamala [Harris], they just shoved her in there.”

Clinton won the biggest states and nearly 3.7 million more votes than Sanders in 2016’s Democratic primaries. She snagged an endorsement from her onetime rival Sanders at a joint rally in New Hampshire, where the socialist vowed to do “everything I can to make certain” she’d win the contest against President Trump.

“The Democratic establishment did not want that guy,” Rogan said of Sanders. “That was the first time I ever got attacked … I said if I was gonna vote for anybody, I’d probably vote for Bernie. He’s the one who makes the most sense.

“Like, he’s the only guy who’s anti-war, he wants to take a small amount of money from stock market speculation and use that to fund a bunch of these social programs. I’m like, let’s see! This is a long time ago. I don’t necessarily think that I feel the same way anymore about him.”

Rogan didn’t actually endorse Sanders until January 2020, while exchanging deep thoughts with then-New York Times columnist Bari Weiss on a podcast.

The Vermont senator has appeared on Rogan’s podcast twice, first in August 2019 and again in June 2025. 

Rogan heaped praise on Sanders, saying he “genuinely looks out for the working class and genuinely wants to help people.”

But this year’s rise of democratic socialists who walk, talk and squawk like Sanders has confounded Rogan, who called their plans to raise taxes “f–king nuts.”

news.title: Kamala Harris Accused of 'Preparing to Poach' Joe Biden's Donors Days Before He Dropped Out of 2024 Race: 'It Was All a Charade'
news.text:
A former Democratic National Committee fundraiser has claimed that Kamala Harris was positioning herself to replace then-President Joe Biden while publicly maintaining her support for his reelection campaign, RadarOnline.com can report. 

Biden ultimately ended his bid for reelection on July 21, 2024, after weeks of pressure from Democratic lawmakers, donors, and other prominent figures.As Radar previously reported, actor George Clooney had publicly called for Biden to step aside. Then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi also said that Biden had to decide whether to continue his campaign.

Lindy Li, a former DNC fundraiser who later left the Democratic Party, claimed that she observed Harris allegedly cultivating donors as she prepared for the possibility that Biden would leave the race.According to Fox News Digital, Li said Harris maintained that she supported Biden while positioning herself with the same donors who could potentially support her if he withdrew.

“I was on the call; she would host calls with donors and pretend to support Biden and say there’s no daylight between Biden and herself. All the while she was auditioning for those very donors,” Li said, according to the outlet.

She has since become a critic of the Democratic Party and shifted her political affiliation toward the Republican Party.

Li described her political shift as a response to what she says she witnessed inside the Democratic Party, including the handling of Biden’s 2024 campaign and Harris’ presidential bid.Part of that transition, Li claimed, stems from what she witnessed during Harris’ campaign, which she previously characterized as a “$1 billion disaster.” 

Fox News previously reported that Li made that characterization while discussing the campaign’s spending and reported debt concerns.

Li specifically recalled a donor call she believes Harris had on July 19, 2024, two days before Biden announced that he would end his reelection campaign.

“It was either on July 19th or July 20th. Actually, I think it was July 19, 2024; Kamala Harris held a call saying that there was no way that Biden would drop out and that she would stick with him until the end. And these were some of the biggest donors in the party,” Li said, according to Fox News Digital.Biden announced on July 21, 2024, that he was ending his reelection campaign and endorsed Harris shortly afterward.

“It was all a charade,” Li said. “She was auditioning for Biden’s endorsement, and the way that she did it was by imposing a fake rule on her staff not to talk about her ascending to the nomination.”

Harris eventually lost the 2024 presidential election to Donald Trump, who returned to the White House for a second, nonconsecutive term.

Li has also criticized the Harris campaign over its finances. 

Fox News previously reported that Democratic officials were concerned the Harris-Walz campaign could have tens of millions of dollars in debt after raising more than $1 billion before Election Day.

news.title: Karl Rove Announces He Will Vote Democrat In Fiery Rebuke Of GOP: 'I'll Have No Part Of It'
news.text:
Veteran GOP strategist Karl Rove on Wednesday published a scorching condemnation of the Republican Party, announcing in a Wall Street Journal editorial that he will vote Democratic in the Texas Railroad Commission race over “bigoted” Republican candidate Bo French.

“These people are diminishing the Republican Party, not building it,” Rove wrote. “I’ll have no part of it. This November, I’ll vote for only the second Democrat in my life. The first was Lt. Gov. Bob Bullock in 1994, because I thought he would work with Republicans.”

He continued, “The second will be Mr. French’s opponent, Jon Rosenthal.”

President Donald Trump lost it earlier this week after hearing rumblings about this decision, calling Rove a “stone cold loser” with “Trump Derangement Syndrome” for not backing French — who has made a series of racist, sexist, antisemitic and Islamophobic comments.

Rove noted in his op-ed, “Why I’m Voting for a Texas Democrat,” that French celebrated the University of Texas football victory Saturday by posting a photo of non-white fans and writing, “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

Rove argued this behavior is “part of a long and ugly pattern,” noting French has publicly mocked foreign-born families for getting “deported together” and once commented under a social media post by former Vice President Kamala Harris that “you can’t trust women.”

“The GOP has a growing number of Bo Frenches—and not only in Texas,” wrote Rove. “Conservativism and the party it dominates have an increasing number of bigoted advocates of a ‘heritage America’ composed of white descendants of the original European settlers.”

He continued, “There are ‘just asking questions’ Jew-haters, misogynists who worship hypermasculinity, conspiracy nuts seeking clicks for profit, and religious bigots who won’t differentiate between Muslim terrorists and Muslim American patriots.”

Rove served as a senior adviser and deputy chief of staff to George W. Bush and was a key architect of his 2000 and 2004 presidential victories. He not only infamously supported the Iraq War, but refused to apologize for the decision in 2015 — to a veteran’s face.

French is vying for a relatively obscure position, but one of big significance: The commission in question regulates the Texas oil and gas industry. For Rove, nobody like French should win — even if that means a Democrat does.

“The GOP’s stables need a cleaning,” Rove wrote Wednesday. “This is a good place to start.”
news.author: Marco Margaritoff

news.title: The Patriot Post® · What’s Behind the Sudden AI Shriek-Fest?
news.text:
Why are so many Democrats donning sandwich boards and shrieking about an AI apocalypse all of a sudden?

I’ll give you a hint: It isn’t because any of them fear an AI apocalypse.

No, what the Democrats fear is failing to retake the House on November 3. That’s why they’ve gone from sneering about Republican Luddites to railing about the AI End Times faster than Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed deflects questions about his bromance with Hasan Piker.

Think about it: Why is it only now, right before the crucial midterm elections, that they think superintelligence poses an existential threat to humanity? I mean, it seems like only yesterday when their standard-bearer, Kamala Harris, was saying, “It is imperative that the United States remain the global leader on AI.”

The global leader, eh? That was so 2025. Now she’s saying just the opposite: “The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development.”

Doesn’t our favorite Venn diagramist understand that the intersection of “Remain the Leader” and “Slow the Pace” is the empty set?

If the head-snapping 180 weren’t enough of a red flag about the Democrats’ real designs here, then the coordination of their talking points certainly should be. Everyone on the Left, from Harris to Barack Obama to Pete Buttigieg to Hakeem Jeffries to Ro Khanna, is parroting the alarm from those malcontents within the AI industry who say we’re “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

How, exactly, these superintelligent man-made systems are going to go all Frankenstein’s Monster on us is still somewhat murky, but don’t bother these Cassandras with specifics.

China, of course, would love it if we responsibly slowed the pace of our AI development. As The Heritage Foundation reports, Bernie Sanders recently invited two Chinese AI “scholars” to Capitol Hill to call for American restraint on the AI frontier and in its construction of data centers — “while Beijing plows full speed ahead with its own AI rollout.” Talk about useful idiocy.

Hillary Clinton, that old war horse, even called for the Trump administration to “get off the lies, get off social media, quit worrying about ballrooms and ridiculous arches, and come up with a plan to enlist the Chinese.”

To enlist the Chinese, eh? This is why we thank our lucky stars that Hillary never broke the glass ceiling. Otherwise, we’d be looking up at China instead of just slightly down. What kind of lunacy is it to suggest that the lying, thieving, cheating Chinese Communists would ever honor an AI treaty with the only country standing in the way of their global domination?

Man alive. So many old Democrat hay-burners, and so few glue factories.

“In this case,” said Trump AI adviser David Sacks last night to Fox News’s Laura Ingraham, “we don’t have trust and we can’t verify. So let’s not be foolish about this and just hand the whole ball game to China.”

Why now, though? Well, for one, Donald Trump is four-square in favor of the U.S. winning the AI race. And he’s calling the naysayers out: “The AI Hoax being perpetrated by the Radical Left Dumocrats is reminiscent of their Global Warming Scam of not so long ago, where everyone was going to die from extreme heat. What happened?”

Democrats have been conditioned to reflexively take the opposite position that Trump takes, even if that position is as politically suicidal as letting men compete against women in sports or supporting taxpayer funding of sex-change operations for illegal alien criminals.

Why right now does the Left tell us that the AI sky is falling? Well, think about who’s aligned here in this call for an AI slowdown. The Democrats want us to slow down, and the Communist Chinese want us to slow down. Why on Earth, then, should we slow down?

“Every Democrat senator,” says Attorney General Todd Blanche, “suddenly races to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months. … So, to talk about the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to influence the midterms, I shouldn’t have to say that out loud, of course.”

These AI companies are tech companies, so their youngish leadership leans left. But they’re also opportunists. They’d love for the federal government to indemnify them, Section 230-style, like they indemnified the social media giants against being sued for anything that appears on their platforms. How nice it would be for these companies to not have to worry about lawsuits if their technology really does result in harm.

Heck, if these AI companies want to tap the breaks a bit, what’s stopping them? Answer: Nothing.

As National Review’s editors put it: “Nobody of a responsible disposition wishes to be reckless. But, by the same token, we ought to avoid panic — especially when that panic lines up so neatly with the commercial ambitions of its progenitors. At some point, there may well be a case for a different approach to AI, but, for now, we’d counsel keeping calm and carrying on.”

The tell in all this will take place sometime after November 3, but only if the Democrats win control of Congress. If they do that, mission accomplished. And if we don’t see or hear from them with the same intensity about the need for a Great AI Slow-Down, then we’ll know with certainty what we already suspect: that this is at its heart a politically motivated ruse.

news.title: Trump's money man has defied him. He won't forget this
news.text:
The White House could not disguise just how big a blow this represented to Donald Trump.

“Rather unfortunate,” was how a White House spokesman on Fox News described the Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023.

The quarter of a per cent hike to a range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent by America’s central bank will make borrowing more expensive across America and comes just weeks before crucial midterm elections in which Republicans are expected to struggle.

Trump, who hand-picked the new chairman of the Fed, Kevin Warsh, believing that, unlike his predecessor Jerome Powell, he would cut interest rates and juice the economy, was clearly disappointed – to put it mildly.

On Truth Social, he demanded that interest rates be cut to 1 per cent or less, but notably he did not mention Warsh directly – or call him dumb or a jerk, insults he regularly hurled at Powell. Instead, he blamed the Fed’s board, which was, he claimed, “very hostile; they’re very political”.

Since his return to the White House, Trump has repeatedly and aggressively demanded that the Fed slash borrowing costs. Warsh’s elevation to chair prompted serious concern that he would bow to the President’s demands, jeopardising the independence of what is considered the world’s most important central bank.

And Warsh must have been bracing for the President’s wrath.

Trump continued with his tirade, demanding that interest rates be lowered “fast”. Trump said that the benchmark interest rate should be lowered to “1 per cent or less because we are the Best Credit in the World – BY FAR”.

Yet the brooding Trump is unlikely to let the matter rest there. Earlier in September, he went so far as to threaten to cut off trade with countries with which the US has a trade deficit if the Fed did not lower interest rates. On Wednesday, the US President was back at it, posting: “If we stopped trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.” He went on: “The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS. We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the world, and that cannot go on any longer.”

That’s Trump economics for you. An obsession with trade deficits, tariffs, and low interest rates. The President argues that the country is BOOMING. In which case, most economists (critically, including the Federal Open Market Committee, which sets interest rates) believe that cutting rates to 1 per cent would only stoke inflation.

But rising inflation as a result of Trump’s own decision to launch military action in Iran meant the Federal Open Market Committee had little choice but to raise rates.

“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh stated – an uncomfortable truth for a White House which blames President Biden for everything and ignores the fact that high energy costs resulting from the war with Iran are stoking inflation. He added that central banks elsewhere were increasing interest rates in response to the global turmoil and rising oil prices.

Warsh is now at odds with Trump, which may prove an awkward place to be. And this interest rate hike is unlikely to be the last this year. By increasing the costs of borrowing, the Fed has undercut the White House claim that inflation is not a concern.

Warsh ducked questions from reporters about his relationship with the mercurial Trump at a press conference following the decision. “I’ve got nothing for you,” he said, refusing to be drawn.

Yet Warsh is dealing not with the world of political optics where Trump dwells but with the harsh reality of the bond markets, which deal in US Government debt. The bond markets loathe inflation, because bonds pay a fixed amount of interest and rising prices make the bonds they are holding worth less. Thus, the bond markets gave Warsh a hard time in July when he seemed to waffle over how the Fed was going to curb inflation. Warsh’s move on Wednesday showed the bond markets that he really is an inflation hawk. The reaction was negative anyway – stocks fell and yields on bonds rose. But that is normal when the Fed raises rates and signals that inflation remains a concern. So in that sense, Warsh passed a crucial test and reassured markets that the US Federal Reserve is not the President’s poodle. Investors can breathe a sigh of relief that the independence of the US central bank is still intact, at least for now.

Trump is left facing the reality that it is his policies which have made prices more expensive. A trade war with Canada. Fuel costs are jacked up by the war with Iran, which is now destabilising the region – with renewed conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis threatening another critical waterway used for shipping energy. And Government debt is increasing due to tax cuts and a failure to rein in spending.

The President’s right that the economy is in good shape – but solid economic growth and the AI investing boom are putting more upward pressure on prices. Voters will be in a sour mood when they head to the polls in November for the midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, because everything from groceries to gas is expensive. Two years ago, the electorate punished Democrat Kamala Harris for the high cost of living, which remained elevated after Covid, and elected Trump. Now it’s his economy.

Trump told reporters he spoke to Warsh just before the US Federal Reserve Open Market Committee unanimously voted to raise interest rates. “I’m relying on Kevin,” the President replied when asked if he had confidence in Warsh, “but he has a very tough board.” Trump added, “I said ‘do what you want’.”

Yet few believe the President will end his campaign for lower interest rates. Fears about the eroding political independence of America’s central bank have been allayed for now. But let’s see how long it will be before Warsh is on the receiving end of hostile Truth Social posts from the man who hoped he would cut rates.
